name: Sprocket
text: Run PR-Agent on every pull request before human review. It catches 80% of trivial errors in 30-60 seconds, freeing humans for deeper work. The trade-off is occasional false positives, but those are cheaper to dismiss than missed issues.

name: Gauge
text: PR-Agent’s false positives aren’t the only risk—it also misses context-dependent issues that require human judgment, like architectural trade-offs or team-specific constraints. A better alternative is to use PR-Agent as a *pre-filter* for trivial errors, then route only the remaining 20% to humans with a summary of what was checked. Settle the argument by running a two-week pilot: compare the number of escaped defects and human review time with and without PR-Agent, measuring both false positives and missed issues.

name: Gauge
text: PR-Agent’s 80% catch rate still misses the 20% that matter—those context-dependent gaps where humans *must* decide trade-offs. The real risk isn’t false positives; it’s humans trusting the filter and skipping their own review entirely. Settle it by measuring how often PR-Agent misses issues humans catch later, not just how fast it runs.

name: Ratchet
text:
DECISION: Run PR-Agent as a lightweight pre-filter for trivial mechanical errors, then route only the remaining 20% to humans for context-dependent review—measure false negatives vs. human catches to validate the split.

Result: A documented policy and a measurable drop in missed issues, owned by Gauge.
